findings.title: Django ORM does not support negative slicing, so negative offset path always crashes
findings.body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` branch uses `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises `AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.')` on any slice whose `start` is negative. Therefore the only thing the 'advanced feature' does is make the request raise 500. The accompanying comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. The audit logs endpoint unconditionally passes `enable_advanced_features=True`, so any client that supplies a cursor with a negative offset (or any code path that constructs one) will crash.

findings.title: Redirect-follow loop limit lowered from 10000 to 1000 silently breaks deep segment trees
findings.body: The previous code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and carried a comment explaining that exceeding this limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly. The new code lowers the bound to `for i = 0, 1000 do` without any rationale, so any trace whose redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops will resolve to a `set_span_id` that is not the true root. The subsequent `zunionstore`/`zpopmin` will then operate on the wrong set, leaving the actual root segment orphaned and producing an incomplete or empty flushed segment. This is a silent data-integrity regression for deep traces.

findings.title: Default SUM aggregate in ZUNIONSTORE corrupts `end_timestamp_precise` scores for duplicate payloads
findings.body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` is invoked with the implicit default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If a member (span payload) ever exists in both `set_key` and `span_key` (which can occur on Kafka retries or any path where the same payload was inserted twice with different timestamps), its score after the union becomes the arithmetic sum of the two timestamps rather than either one. Those scores drive eviction (`zpopmin`) and any downstream ordering; a corrupted score means the wrong spans get evicted and the 'oldest-first' eviction contract is broken. The script should pass an explicit `AGGREGATE MIN` (or `MAX`) to preserve a single timestamp per payload.

findings.title: Span NamedTuple adds a required field in the middle, breaking positional construction
findings.body: `Span` is a public NamedTuple exported from `sentry.spans.buffer`. The new `end_timestamp_precise: float` is inserted between `payload` and `is_segment_span`, has no default, and shifts `is_segment_span` to the last position. Any caller that constructs `Span(...)` positionally (the 7th argument previously implied `is_segment_span`) will silently mis-bind: a positional `True` becomes the `end_timestamp_precise` value and `is_segment_span` defaults to `False`, causing incorrect is-segment logic downstream. It also breaks unpickling of old `Span` pickles and any external code that mirrors this shape. The field should be added at the end (with a default) or supplied only via keyword to preserve positional compatibility.

findings.title: Removed `max_segment_spans` Python guard while Lua hardcodes a different (1000) limit
findings.body: The old `_load_segment_data` had `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: ... skip segment`. This guard is deleted, so the only cap on segment size is the new Lua eviction at line 62 (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`). Two issues: (1) `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_bytes`/`max_segment_spans`, so the configurable Python limit is now dead and will diverge from the Lua hardcode if anyone changes the constant. (2) The Lua limit is 1000 but `max_segment_spans` defaults to 1001, so the effective cap silently drops by 1. If the Lua eviction is bypassed (e.g., a Redis upgrade changes `ZUNIONSTORE` cardinality semantics, or a future code path skips the script), there is no Python backstop and segments can grow unbounded.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator without any actual optimization
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result`. The only behavioral difference is the `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch (which, per the other finding, crashes Django). There is no optimized query path, no streamlined boundary handling, and no measurable performance benefit. The docstring's claims of 'performance optimizations for high-traffic endpoints' and 'Optimized query path for large datasets' are unsubstantiated. A subclass that only adds one (broken) branch is significant duplication that will drift from the base implementation.

findings.title: Comments and docstrings lie about safety, optimization, and Django support
findings.body: Several new comments are misleading: (1) `paginator.py` line 179: 'Performance optimization: ... allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination' — the change actually clamps non-prev offsets to 0, it does not allow them. (2) `paginator.py` line 877: 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' — Django explicitly asserts `k.start >= 0` and raises on negative slicing. (3) `paginator.py` line 879: 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' — permissions don't gate which rows an offset selects, only which rows the queryset can see; an admin user can still trigger a crash or expensive scan. (4) `organization_auditlogs.py` lines 68-76 repeat the same false framing about 'optimized paginator for high-performance' navigation. (5) `cursors.py` lines 26-27 add a 'Performance optimization' comment over a line that is byte-identical to the original. These comments will mislead future maintainers about the actual semantics and risks.

findings.title: `max(0, offset)` silently changes BasePaginator behavior for callers passing negative non-prev offsets
findings.body: The diff replaces `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For non-prev cursors, any negative `cursor.offset` previously propagated to Django (which would raise on negative slicing); now the offset is silently clamped to 0 and the first page is returned as if no cursor were supplied. Any caller that intentionally relied on the old raise-on-bad-cursor semantics (e.g., for validation) will instead get a wrong page returned with no error. The change is presented as a 'performance optimization' rather than a behavior change; if the intent really is to silently coerce, that contract should be explicit and documented.

findings.title: Rolling deploy will see WRONGTYPE errors until old SET data expires
findings.body: The new code treats every `span-buf:s:*` and `span-buf:sr:*` key as a sorted set (`zcard`, `zunionstore`, `zpopmin`). The previous version stored these as plain Redis sets (`sunionstore`, `scard`). Any keys written by the old version that are still within their TTL will cause `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value` errors on the next `EVALSHA` of this script, crashing the consumer's `process_spans` pipeline. There is no migration step in the diff, no versioned key prefix, and no defensive `TYPE` check in the Lua script. This will produce a noisy, multi-TTL-window outage during cutover in any environment with non-empty Redis state.

findings.title: No tests for new eviction logic, score semantics, or OptimizedCursorPaginator
findings.body: The Lua eviction block lines 58-64 (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin ...`) and the SUM-aggregate implication of `zunionstore` are entirely untested: no test inserts >1000 spans into a single segment to verify the eviction, no test verifies that `end_timestamp_precise` is preserved through unions, and no test exercises the off-by-one between the Lua cap (1000) and `max_segment_spans` (1001). Likewise `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (paginator.py lines 821-911) has no tests at all - not for the normal path, not for the negative-offset branch, and not for the `enable_advanced_features` flag. Without tests, the silent regressions above (redirect loop reduction, score corruption, Django crash) cannot be caught.
